variants.title: Give each part its job
variants.context: Function calling is a pattern in which a language model proposes a named tool and structured arguments, then application code decides whether and how to execute that proposal. The tool might read an order, calculate a price, reserve inventory, or send a message.
variants.prompt: From the lesson section “A tool contract has two boundaries”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Name and description
pairs.detail: State what the tool does, when to use it, when not to use it, and what its result means.
pairs.explanation: State what the tool does, when to use it, when not to use it, and what its result means. Ambiguous tools create routing errors before validation starts.

pairs.label: Input schema
pairs.detail: Declare types, required fields, enums, ranges, formats, and whether unknown properties are rejected.
pairs.explanation: Declare types, required fields, enums, ranges, formats, and whether unknown properties are rejected. Keep arguments smaller than the underlying API.

pairs.label: Execution policy
pairs.detail: Bind the call to identity, tenant, task, permission, risk, budget, and confirmation.
pairs.explanation: Bind the call to identity, tenant, task, permission, risk, budget, and confirmation. These checks use trusted application context, not model-supplied claims.

pairs.label: Result contract
pairs.detail: Return bounded fields, stable status codes, provenance, and side-effect identifiers.
pairs.explanation: Return bounded fields, stable status codes, provenance, and side-effect identifiers. Do not dump raw internal records back into the context window.

variants.hint: Give each part the one job only it can do, then rule out the rest. Function calling matters because generated text can now influence real systems.
variants.explanation: Each part has a distinct responsibility. Name and description: State what the tool does, when to use it, when not to use it, and what its result means. Input schema: Declare types, required fields, enums, ranges, formats, and whether unknown properties are rejected. Execution policy: Bind the call to identity, tenant, task, permission, risk, budget, and confirmation. Result contract: Return bounded fields, stable status codes, provenance, and side-effect identifiers.

variants.prompt: From the lesson section “Execute proposals as a state machine”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Parse and correlate
pairs.detail: Capture the provider's call ID, tool name, raw arguments, conversation turn, and task identity.
pairs.explanation: Capture the provider's call ID, tool name, raw arguments, conversation turn, and task identity. Reject malformed or unknown calls.

pairs.label: Validate and authorize
pairs.detail: Apply schema, identity, tenant, permission, approval, budget, and risk checks before obtaining an execution credential.
pairs.explanation: Apply schema, identity, tenant, permission, approval, budget, and risk checks before obtaining an execution credential.

pairs.label: Execute with a deadline
pairs.detail: Pass only validated arguments, use least-privilege credentials, and attach an idempotency key to supported writes.
pairs.explanation: Pass only validated arguments, use least-privilege credentials, and attach an idempotency key to supported writes.

pairs.label: Observe and continue
pairs.detail: Store status, latency, side-effect ID, and bounded result.
pairs.explanation: Store status, latency, side-effect ID, and bounded result. Then return the matching tool result or structured error to the model.

Validate and authorize: Apply schema, identity, tenant, permission, approval, budget, and risk checks before obtaining an execution credential. Execute with a deadline: Pass only validated arguments, use least-privilege credentials, and attach an idempotency key to supported writes. Observe and continue: Store status, latency, side-effect ID, and bounded result.

variants.title: Give each part its job
variants.context: Function calling is a pattern in which a language model proposes a named tool and structured arguments, then application code decides whether and how to execute that proposal. The tool might read an order, calculate a price, reserve inventory, or send a message.
variants.prompt: From the lesson section “Treat timeouts as unknown outcomes”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Read-only call
pairs.detail: A repeated lookup creates no external mutation, though it still consumes capacity and may observe a newer state.
pairs.explanation: A repeated lookup creates no external mutation, though it still consumes capacity and may observe a newer state.

pairs.label: Idempotent write
pairs.detail: The caller sends a stable idempotency key.
pairs.explanation: The caller sends a stable idempotency key. The service stores the first outcome and returns it for duplicate attempts instead of applying the effect again.

pairs.label: Non-idempotent write
pairs.detail: After an ambiguous timeout, query authoritative state or route to review.
pairs.explanation: After an ambiguous timeout, query authoritative state or route to review. Blind retry can create a second message, booking, or payment.

variants.prompt: What is the core authority boundary in function calling?
